subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The US–Taliban agreement that Pakistan helped facilitate was signed at Doha in:
explanation: The Doha Agreement of 29 February 2020 set out the timetable for the withdrawal of US forces from Afghanistan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The proposed Uzbekistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan railway would link Termez with:
explanation: The trans-Afghan line would run from Termez through Mazar-i-Sharif and Kabul to Peshawar.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Pressler Amendment made US aid to Pakistan conditional on:
o: certification that Pakistan did not possess a nuclear explosive device
explanation: When the US President stopped certifying in 1990, economic and military aid to Pakistan was cut off.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The United States designated Pakistan a ‘major non-NATO ally’ in:
explanation: The designation in 2004 recognised Pakistan’s role in the war on terror after 9/11.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Kerry–Lugar–Berman Act (2009) authorised US civilian assistance to Pakistan of:
explanation: The act tripled non-military aid to about $1.5 billion a year for five years, with conditions that caused controversy in Pakistan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: After the Salala check-post attack of November 2011, Pakistan responded by:
explanation: Pakistan blocked NATO convoys to Afghanistan for seven months and had US personnel vacate Shamsi airbase.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The US Coalition Support Fund paid Pakistan for:
o: resettling Afghan refugees in the US
explanation: The CSF reimbursed Pakistan’s logistical and military costs in support of US-led operations after 2001.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The first Pakistan–Russia joint military exercise, held in 2016, was named:
explanation: Druzhba (‘friendship’) was a joint special forces exercise, marking a thaw in Pakistan–Russia relations.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Pakistan Stream Gas Pipeline from Karachi to Punjab is a joint project with:
explanation: The pipeline, formerly the North–South Gas Pipeline, was agreed with Russia to carry imported LNG inland.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: In Pakistan’s security debates, the doctrine of ‘strategic depth’ is most associated with:
explanation: The idea held that a friendly Afghanistan would give Pakistan depth against India on its eastern front.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan conducted its first nuclear tests at Chagai on:
explanation: Pakistan tested on 28 May 1998, about two weeks after India’s tests of 11 and 13 May; the day is marked as Youm-e-Takbeer.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The nuclear tests of 28 May 1998 were carried out in the:
explanation: The first set of tests took place inside tunnels in the Ras Koh Hills of Chagai district, Balochistan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s second nuclear test on 30 May 1998 was conducted in the:
explanation: After the 28 May tests at Ras Koh, a further device was tested on 30 May in the Kharan desert (now Washuk district).

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s nuclear tests of May 1998 were a response to:
explanation: India’s five tests at Pokhran on 11 and 13 May 1998 prompted Pakistan to demonstrate its own capability.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The decision to pursue a nuclear weapons capability is traditionally dated to a meeting of scientists held in January 1972 at:
explanation: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto met Pakistani scientists at Multan on 20 January 1972, soon after the loss of East Pakistan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission was established in:
explanation: PAEC was set up in 1956 to promote peaceful uses of atomic energy and later played a central role in the weapons programme.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Khan Research Laboratories are located at:
explanation: KRL at Kahuta, near Rawalpindi, developed uranium enrichment under Dr Abdul Qadeer Khan and was later renamed after him.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s first research reactor, PARR-1, began operating in 1965 at:
explanation: The US-supplied Pakistan Atomic Research Reactor-1 at the Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science and Technology went critical in 1965.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: NESCOM of Pakistan stands for:
explanation: NESCOM, created in 2001, oversees missile development and other strategic engineering projects.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The National Command Authority, which controls Pakistan’s strategic nuclear forces, is chaired by the:
o: Chairman Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee
explanation: Under the NCA Act 2010, the Prime Minister chairs the National Command Authority; earlier the President held the chair.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Strategic Plans Division serves as the secretariat of the:
explanation: The SPD, set up in 1999–2000, manages policy, security and planning for the nuclear forces on behalf of the NCA.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The National Command Authority was established in:
explanation: The NCA was formed in February 2000; the NCA Act of 2010 later gave it statutory backing.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Which of the following treaties has Pakistan not signed?
explanation: Pakistan has refused to join the NPT as a non-nuclear state, like India, while it is party to the CWC, BWC and the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s position on the Fissile Material Cut-off Treaty (FMCT) is that:
o: the ban on nuclear testing should first be lifted
only plutonium production should be banned
the treaty should apply to non-nuclear states only
pre-existing stockpiles should be included in the treaty
explanation: Pakistan argues that a treaty banning only future production would freeze the existing asymmetry in fissile material with India.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s declared nuclear policy is based on:
explanation: Pakistan describes its posture as credible minimum deterrence, later elaborated as full-spectrum deterrence, and has not adopted a no-first-use pledge.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan proposed a Nuclear Weapon Free Zone in South Asia at the UN General Assembly in:
explanation: Pakistan tabled the proposal after India’s 1974 nuclear explosion and pursued it at the UN for many years.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Which of the following is a Pakistani cruise missile?
explanation: Babur (Hatf-VII) is a ground-launched cruise missile; Ghauri, Shaheen and Ghaznavi are ballistic missiles.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Which Pakistani surface-to-surface ballistic missile is designed to deliver multiple warheads using MIRV technology?
explanation: Ababeel, first tested in January 2017, is designed to carry multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Nasr (Hatf-IX) is best known as a:
explanation: Nasr is a short-range, nuclear-capable tactical missile intended to deter limited incursions.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Babur-3, first tested in January 2017, is a:
explanation: Babur-3 gives Pakistan a sea-based second-strike option; it was test-fired from an underwater platform in the Indian Ocean.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Ra’ad (Hatf-VIII) is Pakistan’s:
explanation: Ra’ad is carried by aircraft and uses stand-off range to strike targets without entering air defences.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Shaheen-III, first tested in 2015, has a declared range of about:
explanation: ISPR announced a range of 2,750 km for the solid-fuelled Shaheen-III, the longest of Pakistan’s tested missiles.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Ghaznavi missile is named after:
explanation: Pakistan names several ballistic missiles after Muslim conquerors of the subcontinent: Ghaznavi, Ghauri and Abdali.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The JF-17 Thunder fighter aircraft was jointly developed by Pakistan and:
explanation: The JF-17 was developed with China’s Chengdu Aircraft Corporation and is assembled at Kamra.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Pakistan Aeronautical Complex is located at:
explanation: PAC Kamra in Attock district manufactures and overhauls aircraft, including the JF-17.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan Ordnance Factories are located at:
explanation: POF Wah, set up in 1951, is Pakistan’s largest producer of conventional arms and ammunition.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Al-Khalid main battle tank is produced at:
explanation: Heavy Industries Taxila builds and rebuilds armoured vehicles; Al-Khalid was developed with China.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s first satellite, Badr-1, was launched in:
explanation: SUPARCO’s Badr-1 was launched on a Chinese Long March rocket in July 1990.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Jinnah Naval Base is located at:
explanation: Jinnah Naval Base at Ormara on the Makran coast was built to reduce the Navy’s dependence on Karachi.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Pakistan Military Academy is located at:
explanation: PMA Kakul near Abbottabad trains army officer cadets; Risalpur has the PAF Academy and Quetta the Command and Staff College.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Kargil conflict took place in:
explanation: Fighting in the Kargil heights of Indian-held Kashmir lasted from May to July 1999.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Operation Gibraltar (1965) aimed at:
explanation: The August 1965 infiltration plan was meant to spark an uprising in Kashmir but escalated into the 1965 war.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: India occupied the Siachen Glacier in 1984 through Operation:
explanation: Operation Meghdoot in April 1984 put Indian troops on the Saltoro Ridge, starting the Siachen conflict.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Which U.S. military operation in 2011 resulted in the death of Osama bin Laden in Pakistan?
explanation: US special forces carried out Operation Neptune Spear at Abbottabad on 2 May 2011 without informing Pakistan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s response to India’s Balakot airstrike in February 2019 was named:
explanation: In Operation Swift Retort on 27 February 2019, the PAF shot down an Indian aircraft and captured its pilot.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Operation Zarb-e-Azb (2014) was launched in:
explanation: The army launched Zarb-e-Azb in June 2014 to clear militant sanctuaries in North Waziristan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Operation Rah-e-Rast (2009) was conducted in:
explanation: Rah-e-Rast cleared Swat and adjoining districts of Taliban control in 2009.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Operation Rah-e-Nijat (2009) was conducted in:
explanation: Launched in October 2009, Rah-e-Nijat targeted the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan’s base in South Waziristan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan started Operation Radd-ul-Fasaad in ______ 2017.
explanation: Radd-ul-Fasaad, launched on 22 February 2017, was a countrywide operation to eliminate residual terrorist networks.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan was formed in 2007 under the leadership of:
explanation: Baitullah Mehsud united several militant groups as the TTP in December 2007; he was killed in 2009.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The terrorist attack on the Army Public School, Peshawar, took place on:
explanation: The attack killed about 150 people, most of them children, and led to the National Action Plan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The National Action Plan against terrorism, adopted in December 2014, consisted of:
explanation: The 20-point NAP, agreed by all parties after the APS attack, covered military courts, banned outfits, madrassa reform, terror financing and FATA reforms.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: NACTA stands for:
o: National Agency for Countering Terrorist Activity
explanation: NACTA coordinates counter-terrorism policy and intelligence among federal and provincial bodies.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: NACTA was given statutory status by an Act of Parliament in:
explanation: NACTA was first set up administratively in 2009; the NACTA Act 2013 put it on a legal footing.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s Anti-Terrorism Act, which set up anti-terrorism courts, was passed in:
explanation: The ATA of 1997, passed under Nawaz Sharif’s second government, remains the main counter-terrorism law.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s first National Security Policy, covering 2022–26, was released in:
explanation: The policy, unveiled in January 2022, placed economic security at the centre of national security.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan was removed from the FATF grey list in:
explanation: After completing its action plans, Pakistan was taken off the list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring in October 2022.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan was last placed on the FATF grey list in:
explanation: The FATF placed Pakistan under increased monitoring in June 2018 with an action plan on terror financing and money laundering.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan is a member of which FATF-style regional body?
explanation: The Asia/Pacific Group on Money Laundering conducts mutual evaluations of Pakistan’s anti-money-laundering regime.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The most widely spoken mother tongue in Pakistan is:
explanation: Successive censuses show Punjabi as the first language of the largest share of Pakistanis; Urdu is the national language and lingua franca.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Brahui, spoken in central Balochistan, belongs to which language family?
explanation: Brahui is a Dravidian language, related to the languages of southern India, though it has borrowed heavily from Balochi.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Shina is spoken mainly in:
explanation: Shina is the main language of Gilgit, Diamer and Astore, and is also spoken in parts of Kohistan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Balti language is closely related to:
explanation: Balti, spoken in Baltistan, is a Tibetic language, reflecting the region’s historical links with Ladakh and Tibet.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Khowar is the main language of:
explanation: Khowar is spoken throughout Chitral and in parts of Ghizer district of Gilgit-Baltistan.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Hindko is spoken mainly in:
explanation: Hindko is the language of Abbottabad, Mansehra and other Hazara districts and of the old city of Peshawar.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Saraiki is spoken mainly in:
explanation: Saraiki is the language of Multan, Bahawalpur, Dera Ghazi Khan and neighbouring districts.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Burushaski, spoken in Hunza, Nagar and Yasin, is notable because it is a:
explanation: Burushaski has no proven relationship to any other language family.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The most populous province of Pakistan is:
explanation: Punjab holds more than half of Pakistan’s population, although Balochistan is the largest province by area.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The largest city of Pakistan by population is:
explanation: Karachi, the country’s main port and commercial centre, is Pakistan’s largest city, followed by Lahore.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s first population census was held in:
explanation: The first census after independence was carried out in 1951; later censuses followed in 1961, 1972, 1981, 1998, 2017 and 2023.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Pakistan’s first digital population census was conducted in:
explanation: The seventh census of 2023 used tablets and online self-enumeration for the first time.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: According to the 2023 census, Pakistan’s population was about:
explanation: The 2023 census counted about 241.5 million people; the 2017 census had recorded about 208 million.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Population censuses in Pakistan are conducted by the:
explanation: The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, under the Planning Ministry, carries out the population and housing censuses.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Benazir Income Support Programme was launched in:
explanation: BISP began in 2008 as an unconditional cash-transfer programme for poor women and remains Pakistan’s largest social safety net.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The University of the Punjab, the oldest university in Pakistan, was founded in:
explanation: The University of the Punjab was established in Lahore in 1882.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Government College, Lahore, was founded in:
explanation: Government College (now GC University) was established in 1864; Allama Iqbal was among its students.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: King Edward Medical University in Lahore traces its origin to a medical school founded in:
explanation: It began as the Lahore Medical School in 1860 and was renamed King Edward Medical College in 1911.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The Higher Education Commission replaced the University Grants Commission in:
explanation: The HEC was set up in 2002 to fund, oversee and accredit universities.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: Allama Iqbal Open University, Islamabad, was established in:
explanation: It was founded in 1974 as the People’s Open University to provide distance education.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
q: The University of Agriculture, one of Pakistan’s leading agricultural universities, is in:
explanation: It grew from the Punjab Agricultural College founded at Lyallpur in 1906 and became a university in 1961.
